name: Sleep to look attractive (beauty sleep research)
lead: Beauty sleep is the idea that getting enough sleep improves how a person looks, and that sleep-deprived faces come across as less healthy and less attractive. It is a staple of appearance advice and looksmaxxing discussion, where adequate sleep is treated as a free way to look more rested, with brighter skin, calmer eyes and a livelier expression.[1][2][3]

Experimental research has tested this directly. In a 2010 BMJ study, 23 adults were photographed after a normal night's sleep and after 31 hours awake, and 65 untrained observers rated the photos; sleep-deprived people were rated as less healthy, more tired and less attractive.[2] A 2013 follow-up in Sleep had 40 observers rate photos of 10 people and reported that sleep-deprived faces showed hanging eyelids, redder and more swollen eyes, darker under-eye circles, paler skin, more wrinkles and droopier mouth corners.[3]

Other work has looked at skin. A 2023 study of total sleep deprivation and repeated partial deprivation reported increased facial skin yellowness that persisted after sleep was restored.[4] Sleep medicine sources also list eye bags, periorbital puffiness and styes among visible signs of sleep loss.[1]

chain: Fewer visible fatigue cues around the eyes, mouth and skin
A healthier, more rested and more attractive appearance
angle.text: Observers in experiments rate rested faces as healthier, less tired and more attractive than the same faces after sleep loss. Followers treat consistent sleep as a baseline for eye area, skin tone and overall freshness.

paras: Reported visible effects of sleep deprivation include eye bags, puffiness around the eyes and styes.[1] Sleep loss is also associated with irritability and slower reactions, which affect presentation beyond the face.[1]

In the 2013 Sleep study, sleep-deprived faces were rated as having hanging eyelids, redder and more swollen eyes, darker circles under the eyes, paler skin, more wrinkles and fine lines, and droopier mouth corners; they also looked sadder, while ratings of rash or tense lips were not affected.[3]

In the 2010 BMJ study, observers rated photos of people after 31 hours awake as less healthy (63 versus 68 on the scale used), more tired (53 versus 44) and less attractive (38 versus 40) than after normal sleep, and lower health ratings tracked higher tiredness and lower attractiveness ratings.[2]

A 2023 study of first impressions found that poorer sleepers socialised less but did not rate others as less attractive, and an fMRI experiment reported altered brain responses to negative social feedback after sleep deprivation.[5]

A 2023 paper reported that both a night without sleep (28 participants) and five nights of 4-hour sleep (10 participants) increased facial skin yellowness, an effect that lingered after sleep was restored; circulating yellow chromophores did not change, and facial redness was unaffected.[4]

Experimental studies have examined how observers rate faces after sleep deprivation, including the 2010 BMJ study of 23 adults and the 2013 Sleep study of 10 faces rated by 40 observers.[2][3] A 2023 study measured facial skin yellowness after total and partial sleep deprivation.[4] These studies used short-term deprivation in small samples.

timeline.event: Axelsson and colleagues publish the BMJ study on perceived health and attractiveness of sleep-deprived people.[2]
Sundelin and colleagues publish a study of facial cues of fatigue in Sleep.[3]
A study reports increased facial skin yellowness after sleep deprivation.[4]

card.summary: The belief that enough sleep makes you look better: visible signs of sleep loss are documented.

quick.overview:
Beauty sleep is the idea that sleep affects how attractive you look.

Documented effects of sleep loss include eye bags and puffiness.
quick.mechanism: People simply sleep enough; sleep loss is associated with visible signs around the eyes.[1]
quick.risks: Sleep loss is linked to cognitive, mood and health effects; no risks of sleeping adequately are described.
